title: Peregrin and the Tidy Hedgehog
markdown:
In Ferncrown, moonbeams kept secrets in the ferns and mushrooms hummed quiet lullabies. Peregrin lived there: a young wizard whose sleeves were always smudged with berry juice and a sparkle of stardust. He clutched a Moonpetal Lantern, pearly light pulsing against his palms. It had to stand on the highest spire of the Glimmering Grove before the moon kissed the horizon.

Tidy the hedgehog bristled beside him, snout twitching, spines ready for a job. “I’ll help, Peregrin! I’ll tidy the path! No stray leaves out of place!” He nudged a large acorn into what he believed was a better position. The acorn rolled back.

“That’s thoughtful, Tidy.” Peregrin’s voice was as calm as a still forest pool. “But perhaps we should just walk. Gently. The forest floor has its own way of being just so.”

They stepped into the Whispering Woods. Ancient trees lifted their branches like wise old arms. Peregrin watched the sky between them, counting the light. Tidy watched the ground, which, in his opinion, was a disgrace.

A tangle of brambles. “Aha!” Spines vibrating, he pushed. Dry leaves and twigs showered the path he had meant to improve. “Oh dear,” Peregrin murmured. “We don’t want to make a mess of it.”

Tidy mistook a patch of damp dew for mud and rolled, emerging dusted in clover green. Then he organised pinecones, rolling them with his nose into a pile at Peregrin’s feet. The pile collapsed. Tidy began again.

From the moss rose a tiny puff of smoke that smelled of cinnamon and toasted honey. A dragon no bigger than a robin blinked up with eyes like flickering embers. One wing was caught in a sticky spiderweb.

“Oh my.” A voice like rustling leaves. “You’re trying to get somewhere quickly. I am Ember. I can’t get free.”

Peregrin knelt, robes settling. He untangled the wing with a touch as soft as new moss. Tidy, mistaking rescue for tidying, patted Ember with his bristly back. A surprised smoky huff.

“Thank you.” Ember flexed. He looked at the lantern, then the sky. “The Moonpetal Lantern. The Grove spire. Before moonset.”

Peregrin nodded. “We are running late.”

Ember beamed, amber warm. “Hop on. My breath can give me a boost. I know a shortcut.”

So Peregrin held the pulsing lantern, Tidy clung to spines that were not designed for flight, and Ember’s cinnamon-scented wings carried them over tangled roots and shadowy hollows. The woods slid beneath like a dark river. Tidy squeezed his eyes shut, then opened them, then tried to tidy the air with his nose and found there was nothing to tidy, which was almost worse.

They landed on the Glimmering Grove spire as the last sliver of sun dipped, orange and purple. Peregrin set the lantern. Pearly light bloomed over ferns and flowers. The Grove became a quiet beacon. Tidy sat very still, green clover still in his spines, and did not push a single leaf.

Peregrin patted him. “You tried your best.”

Tidy looked at the lit grove. He had not tidied the path. He had scattered it, rolled in it, piled pinecones on it. Peregrin had been patient anyway, and Ember’s wing was free, and the lantern was where it needed to be, exactly when the moon arrived. That, Tidy decided, would have to do for tidy.
